# DISTRIBUTIONS {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(theme_ggp2g(
    base_size = 15))
bare_theme <- theme(plot.title = element_blank(),
                    plot.subtitle = element_blank(),
                    plot.caption = element_blank(),
                    axis.title = element_blank(),
                    axis.text = element_blank(),
                    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
                    strip.text = element_blank(),
                    strip.background = element_blank(),
                    legend.position = "none")
```

The graphs in this part show the form the numbers in a column take.[^distributions] They help us see if the numbers come together in the middle and fall off the same way on both sides, if they run out farther on one side, and how many of them are far out at the ends.[^dist-shape]

## Overlapping histograms

[Overlapping histograms](overlapping_histograms.qmd) put one histogram for each group in the same graph, one on top of the other. We can see through the bars, so it's clear where the groups cover each other and where they don't.[^alpha] Overlapping histograms work well for comparing two or three groups, but get too full with more. A color for each group shows which bars are which.[^legend]

```{r}
#| label: part_overlapping_histograms
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
tamagotchi_pets <- tibble(
  pet_id = 1:450,
  care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150)) |>
  mutate(care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
         lifespan_days = round(rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2,
           scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13,
                     Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), 1))
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
(
  ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
    labs_ovrlp_hist
) +
  fmggp2::theme_tamagotchi(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Overlapping frequency polygons

[Overlapping frequency polygons](overlapping_frequency_polygons.qmd) use one line for each group, and each line shows how many of the group's numbers fall in each part of the number line.[^ovrlp-fp] Because they use lines and not bars, frequency polygons can compare more groups than overlapping histograms without the groups covering each other. The form of each line shows where the middle of the group is, how far out its numbers reach, and if it runs out farther on one side.[^fp-shape] A color for each group shows which line is which.[^legend]

```{r}
#| label: part_overlapping_frequency_polygons
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1990)
soaker_shots <- tibble(
  shot_id = 1:600,
  model = rep(c("SS 50", "SS 100", "CPS 2000"), each = 200)) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("SS 50", "SS 100", "CPS 2000")),
         avg_range = c(`SS 50` = 25, `SS 100` = 35,
                       `CPS 2000` = 45)[as.character(model)],
         range_ft = round(rnorm(n(), mean = avg_range,
                                sd = 0.12 * avg_range), 1)) |>
  select(shot_id, model, range_ft)
labs_ovrlp_freq_poly <- labs(
  title = "Super Soaker range",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "200 shots from each model",
  x = "Range (feet)",
  color = "Model")
ggp2_ovrlp_freq_poly <- ggplot(data = soaker_shots,
       aes(x = range_ft,
           group = model)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = model), binwidth = 2, linewidth = 1)
(
  ggp2_ovrlp_freq_poly +
    labs_ovrlp_freq_poly
) +
  fmggp2::theme_supersoaker(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Overlapping dot plots

[Overlapping dot plots](overlapping_dot_plots.qmd) build up one dot for every number in each group along the same axis.[^ovrlp-dot] Each dot is one number, so we can find how many there are, dot by dot, and see where dots come together, places with no dots, and numbers far from the rest in each group.[^dot-patterns] Dot plots work best with small or middle sized sets of data. A color for each group shows which dots are which.[^legend]

```{r}
#| label: part_overlapping_dot_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1992)
goosebumps_readers <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:120,
  grade = rep(c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade"), each = 40)) |>
  mutate(grade = factor(grade,
           levels = c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade")),
         books_read = rpois(n(), lambda = c(`3rd grade` = 3, `4th grade` = 6,
                                            `5th grade` = 9)[as.character(grade)]))
labs_ovrlp_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Goosebumps books read",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "40 students in each grade, one school year",
  x = "Books read",
  fill = "Grade")
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot <- ggplot(data = goosebumps_readers,
    aes(x = books_read,
        fill = grade)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    method = "histodot",
    binwidth = 1,
    binpositions = "all",
    stackgroups = TRUE)
(
  ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot +
    labs_ovrlp_dotplot
) +
  fmggp2::theme_goosebumps(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Beeswarm plots

A [beeswarm plot](beeswarm_plots.qmd) shows every number as a point, and moves the points so they don't cover each other. Where many numbers are close together, the points move out to the sides, so how wide each group of points is shows where most of the numbers fall.[^swarm] Beeswarm plots are a good way to compare where the numbers fall in different groups while we still see each point. Each group gets its own set of points, most often along the `x` axis.

```{r}
#| label: part_beeswarm_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1989)
tetris_games <- tibble(
  game_id = 1:240,
  player = rep(c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert"), each = 80)) |>
  mutate(player = factor(player, levels = c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert")),
         lines_cleared = rnbinom(n(), size = 5,
           mu = c(Casual = 25, Regular = 60,
                  Expert = 120)[as.character(player)]))
# ggp2_beeswarm ----
labs_beeswarm <- labs(
    title = "Tetris",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    subtitle = "Lines cleared in 80 games by each player",
    x = "Player",
    y = "Lines cleared")
ggp2_beeswarm <-  ggplot(data = tetris_games,
    aes(x = player,
        y = lines_cleared,
        color = player)) +
    ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(
        alpha = 2 / 3,
        size = 1.15,
        cex = 1.5,
        dodge.width = 1,
        show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(1, 1))) +
    labs_beeswarm
(
  ggp2_beeswarm
) +
  fmggp2::theme_tetris(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Overlapping and stacked density plots

[Overlapping and stacked density plots](overlapping_stacked_density_plots.qmd) use one line for each group that shows where its numbers fall.[^ovrlp-density] In overlapping density plots we can see through each group, so it's clear where the groups share the same values.[^alpha] Stacked density plots put each group on top of the ones under it, so the top line shows all the groups together.[^stack] Density plots take away the small ups and downs we see in histograms, which makes the forms easier to compare.[^noise] A color for each group shows which line is which.[^legend]

```{r}
#| label: part_overlapping_stacked_density_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1998)
pager_messages <- tibble(
  msg_id = 1:300,
  model = rep(c("RIM 950", "PageWriter"), times = c(180, 120))) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("RIM 950", "PageWriter")),
         msg_length = round(if_else(model == "RIM 950",
           rnorm(n(), mean = 45, sd = 8),
           rnorm(n(), mean = 30, sd = 10))))
labs_ovrlp_density <- labs(
  subtitle = "position = 'identity'",
  x = "Message length (characters)",
  fill = "Pager model")
ggp2_ovrlp_density <- ggplot(data = pager_messages,
       aes(x = msg_length,
           fill = model)) +
      geom_density(alpha = 1/3, bounds = c(0, Inf))

ovrlp_density <- ggp2_ovrlp_density +
  labs_ovrlp_density +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

labs_stack_density <- labs(
  subtitle = "position = 'stack'",
  x = "Message length (characters)",
  fill = "Pager model")
ggp2_stack_density <- ggplot(data = pager_messages,
       aes(x = msg_length,
           after_stat(count),
           fill = model)) +
      geom_density(position = "stack",
                   alpha = 1/3,
                   bounds = c(0, Inf))
stack_density <- ggp2_stack_density +
  labs_stack_density +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
(
  ovrlp_density + stack_density +
      patchwork::plot_layout(ncol = 1)
) &
  fmggp2::theme_pager(base_size = 12) &
  bare_theme
```

## Ridgeline plots

A [ridgeline plot](ridgeline_plots.qmd) shows a density line for each group in its own row, and each line reaches a little way up into the row above it.[^ridgeline] The rows share the same `x` axis, so we can compare the middle, how wide they are, and the form of many groups at once.[^center-spread] Ridgeline plots help most when there are too many groups for overlapping density plots. Each group gets its own row along the `y` axis.

```{r}
#| label: part_ridgeline_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggridges)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1998)
squeezit_drinks <- tibble(
  bottle_id = 1:360,
  flavor = rep(c("Tropical", "Blue raspberry", "Strawberry", "Green punch", "Orange", "Cherry"),
              each = 60)) |>
  mutate(flavor = factor(flavor, levels = c("Cherry", "Orange", "Green punch", "Strawberry",
                                          "Blue raspberry", "Tropical")),
         avg_seconds = c(Tropical = 40, `Blue raspberry` = 32, Strawberry = 26, `Green punch` = 22,
                      Orange = 18, Cherry = 12)[as.character(flavor)],
         seconds_to_finish = pmax(1, round(rgamma(n(), shape = 2.5,
                                                  scale = avg_seconds / 2.5)))) |>
  select(bottle_id, flavor, seconds_to_finish)
labs_ridges <- labs(
  title = "Squeezit",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Seconds to squeeze out a whole bottle",
  x = "Seconds to finish",
  y = "Flavor", fill = "Flavor")
ggp2_ridges <- ggplot(data = squeezit_drinks,
       aes(x = seconds_to_finish,
           y = flavor,
        fill = flavor)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
(
  ggp2_ridges +
    labs_ridges
) +
  fmggp2::theme_squeezit(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Grouped box plots

[Grouped box plots](grouped_box_plots.qmd) show a box plot for each group side by side. Each box shows the middle number and the middle half of the numbers, the lines out from the box reach the smallest and largest numbers that are not far from the rest, and points past the ends of those lines show numbers far from the rest.[^box-parts] Grouped box plots fit many groups in very little space. The groups run along one axis and the numbers run along the other.

```{r}
#| label: part_grouped_box_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1985)
oregon_trail <- tibble(
  party_id = 1:300,
  profession = rep(c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer"), each = 100)) |>
  mutate(profession = factor(profession,
           levels = c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer")),
         median_days = c(Banker = 140, Carpenter = 155,
                         Farmer = 170)[as.character(profession)],
         days_to_oregon = round(rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(median_days),
                                       sdlog = 0.2))) |>
  select(party_id, profession, days_to_oregon)
labs_grp_boxplots <- labs(
  title = "The Oregon Trail",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon",
  x = "Profession", fill = "Profession",
  y = "Days to reach Oregon")
ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
        fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
(
  ggp2_grp_boxplots +
    labs_grp_boxplots
) +
  fmggp2::theme_oregontrail(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Grouped violin plots

[Grouped violin plots](grouped_violin_plots.qmd) show a violin plot for each group side by side. Each violin is a density line shown on both sides of a center line, so how wide it is shows how often each value comes up in that group.[^violin-width] Violins show forms that a box plot doesn't show, such as two high points in the same group.[^peaks] The groups run along one axis, and often a color for each group shows which is which.

```{r}
#| label: part_grouped_violin_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
aim_buddies <- tibble(
  user_id = 1:450,
  school = rep(c("Middle school", "High school", "College"), each = 150)) |>
  mutate(school = factor(school,
           levels = c("Middle school", "High school", "College")),
         buddies = case_when(
           school == "Middle school" ~ rpois(n(), lambda = 20),
           school == "High school" ~ round(rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(45),
                                                  sdlog = 0.45)),
           TRUE ~ round(if_else(runif(n()) < 0.7,
                                rnorm(n(), mean = 60, sd = 10),
                                rnorm(n(), mean = 150, sd = 20)))))
labs_grp_violin <- labs(
  title = "AOL Instant Messenger",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Buddy list sizes for 150 users at each level of school",
  x = "School", fill = "School",
  y = "Buddies")
ggp2_grp_violin <- ggplot(data = aim_buddies,
       aes(x = school,
           y = buddies,
        fill = school)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
(
  ggp2_grp_violin +
    labs_grp_violin
) +
  fmggp2::theme_aim(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Raincloud plots

A [raincloud plot](raincloud_plots.qmd) shows the same data in three ways: half of a density line (the cloud), a box plot, and a point for each number (the rain).[^raincloud] Together they show the form of the numbers, a few numbers that stand for all of them, and every number.[^summary] Raincloud plots are a good choice for comparing groups, or the same thing looked at more than one time, when we don't want to cover up any of the data.[^repeated] Each group gets its own cloud and rain, and a color for each group shows which is which.

```{r}
#| label: part_raincloud_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggdist)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1994)
rzone_games <- tibble(
  player_id = 1:240,
  game = rep(c("Racing", "Fighting", "Shooter"), each = 80)) |>
  mutate(game = factor(game,
           levels = c("Racing", "Fighting", "Shooter")),
         seconds = round(rlnorm(n(), sdlog = 0.5,
           meanlog = log(c(Racing = 15, Fighting = 30,
                           Shooter = 60)[as.character(game)])), 1))
labs_raincloud_2 <- ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Tiger R-Zone",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    x = "Seconds to clear the first level",
    y = "Game")
(
  ggplot(rzone_games,
      aes(x = seconds, y = game)) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = game),
      notch = TRUE,
      notchwidth = 0.9,
      width = .15,
      outlier.shape = NA) +
    ggdist::stat_halfeye(aes(fill = game),
      adjust = 0.6, # shape = adjust * density estimator
      .width = 0, # can use probabilities or 0
      point_colour = NA, # removes the point in center
      orientation = "horizontal", # like the box plot
      height = 0.5, # height of curve
      justification = -0.3) + # shift vertically above box
      geom_point(aes(fill = game),
          shape = 21,
          color = "#ffffff",
          alpha = 1/3, size = 1.8,
      position = position_jitter(
        seed = 321,
        height = .07)) +
      theme(legend.position = "none") +
      labs_raincloud_2
) +
  fmggp2::theme_rzone(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

[^distributions]: These graphs display the shape of a variable's values (its distribution).

[^dist-shape]: Good for assessing [normality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution), [skewness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness), [kurtosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis), etc.

[^alpha]: The fill is partially transparent (`alpha`), so we can see where the groups overlap and where they separate.

[^legend]: Color separates the groups.

[^ovrlp-fp]: A line for each group's counts across the bins of a numeric variable.

[^fp-shape]: The shape of each line shows the center, spread, and skew of each group.

[^ovrlp-dot]: A dot for every observation, stacked in each group on the same axis.

[^dot-patterns]: Dot plots let us count observations directly and see clusters, gaps, and outliers; they work best with small to moderate datasets.

[^swarm]: The points are arranged so they don't overlap and spread sideways where values are crowded, so the width of the swarm shows where values are concentrated.

[^ovrlp-density]: A smooth density curve for each group.

[^stack]: Stacked densities place each group on top of the others to show the total.

[^noise]: Density plots smooth over the noise in histograms, which makes the overall shapes easier to compare.

[^ridgeline]: Each group's density curve sits in its own row, slightly overlapping the row above it.

[^center-spread]: The center, spread, and shape of each group.

[^box-parts]: Each box shows the median and the middle half of the values (the interquartile range), the whiskers reach the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box, and points beyond the whiskers show unusual values (outliers).

[^violin-width]: Each violin is a mirrored density curve, so its width shows how common each value is.

[^peaks]: Two peaks (a bimodal distribution).

[^raincloud]: A half density curve (the cloud), a box plot, and the individual points (the rain).

[^summary]: The shape of the distribution, its summary statistics, and every observation.

[^repeated]: Repeated measurements.
